rules_text:
Rules summary Overview Manage the market whilst making sure to keep hold of high value destinations Each destination has 11 cards, 10 numbered 3 to 12, then one extra depending on the color: grey 8, blue 7, yellow 6, green 5 and red 4, making a total of 55 cards. In two and three player games cards with value 10,11,12 are removed. Depending on number of players a set number of cards are removed (without revealing) at a set start of game and cards are drawn to Market. Game Setup Number of Players 2 3 4 5 6 Cards removed at start of game 9 1 4 7 1 Initial marketing cards 3 3 3 3 0 Turn Draft 1 of 3 cards into your hand, then pass the remaining Draft 1 of the 2 cards into your hand, then the remaining goes into the central Market In two player games at the end of the round the top card of the deck is revealed and placed into the central Market. Game End The game ends when the deck runs out Out of all the 5 destinations, the three in the Market with the highest score will score positively Whilst the 2 in the Market with the lowest score will score negatively Reveal your hand cards and score each according to its value and whether it is a positive or negative scoring destination as depicted by the Market The player with the most points, wins!

[Rating: 3/10] Quick card drafter where you are secretly collecting shares in one of 5 suits. Since the last card you don't draft is what adds to the table to determine the total value of that suit, you have some influence and difficult decisions (keeping a high card will hurt you more if that suit loses, but if you don't keep it, that suit might then beat out another suit you're invested in), but for my small brain it still seems very unpredictable what the final 3 top suits will be. [Rating: 4/10] 5 rounds of pick and pass, to a stock market scoring mechanic. Would be better if you didn't pass the cards and got to split the 3 cards immediately. As it is now you have very little control and feels forced and random.

[Rating: 4/10] Just too chaotic. In theory the game has got a LOT of potential. If you keep a card, you are also devaluing it's end game value. So you're left with a tough choice. However, in practice, it's just not feasible to plan out your best choice and so it just ends up being dumb luck.  And sometimes, there is no real choice. At the beginning, if you're dealt 2 cards of the same kind, you have to take one. Passing someone a pair is strategically stupid.   Maybe it's that the game doesn't work at 3 players? [Rating: 5/10] After two plays at 2 with the advanced variant, I think everything this game does at least one other game does better—but not necessarily in 10 minutes. Agency feels low, excitement doesn't feel high to make up for it. Sort of curious to try with more players, sort of indifferent. Card backs are very pleasant to look at. Middling cardstock and the standard tuckbox doesn't accommodate sleeves.  Comparisons that come to mind: Arboretum, Between Two Cities, Botswana, Fantasy Realms, Modern Art, Red7, Rummy, Songbirds

[Rating: 5/10] I like how board games can be diluted or distilled. For example, 7 Wonders is your mid drafting game and Sushi Go is the light drafting game. Forks makes drafting even lighter - you only draft from 3 cards and you draft one of 5 types of cards. The premise is neat but it's too short to let the game develop - it makes the draft picking feel too random and inconsequential.
